category_rulings.category: a translation made for the receiving church
category_rulings.reason: Major when the receiving church's own leaders, or one of its houses, make or commission it for common use (Scripture, worship, rule, copies for its bishops); minor when one writer translates for readers. Translating is more than reading only when a church takes the text into use.

category_rulings.category: appealing to or quoting an authority
category_rulings.reason: Citing a name shows regard, not adoption; major only when the lines show the later side making the teaching its own, as Calvin says of Augustine.

category_rulings.category: set reading in a monastic rule
category_rulings.reason: A rule that fixes a text as the community's reading has written it into practice; a teacher's advice to read is minor.
Confirmation gives the rule standing law and settles the body's form, a settlement beyond the request itself.

category_rulings.category: a ruling in a letter with no sign it was carried out
category_rulings.reason: A letter shows a decision sent, not a rule changed; council canons and imperial laws differ because they are themselves the enactment.

Can carry a major when the act reported is public (a council, law, deposition, expulsion) and the sentence names the witness where it is disputed; a private exchange reported only by a party is minor.
A canon that sets how a church is ruled, or on what terms a group is received, is a rule changed, provided it acts on this link's parties.

category_rulings.category: an exile or suspension soon reversed
category_rulings.reason: Not lasting; the same holds for any change the sources show undone soon after (the Oea reading, the Greek patriarch at Antioch).

category_rulings.category: evidence only in a secondary note
category_rulings.reason: Major only when the reviewed note states the result and the secondary text is vendored and the cited lines show it; the ruling ties every major mark to a source the review checks, which a file-less secondary is not.
The test names councils, canons, synods and laws; one bishop's sentence is part of the quarrel unless a body acted with him or a source shows the exclusion held.

category_rulings.category: a compilation such as the Philokalia
category_rulings.reason: Major when a primary line shows the receiving movement's own collection carrying the text for its practice; a library, catalogue or editor's credit alone is minor.
The window is the evidence rule; a result outside it goes to wants, not to the map.

category_rulings.category: one event carried on two links
category_rulings.reason: Major on each link whose party the act names or is aimed at in its own words; minor where it only touches a person who also belongs to the other link, or where a by-type link between the same pair already carries the event.

category_rulings.category: standing jurisdiction (a church receiving its head bishop from another)
category_rulings.reason: Major only when a source shows the arrangement being made (a canon, a grant); a description of standing practice is minor.

category_rulings.category: a result dated after one party's span
category_rulings.reason: The act must fall within the linked movements' own time to be their result.

decisions.outcome: Jerome had marked his earlier Latin Job with Origen's asterisks and obeli, restoring some seven or eight hundred lines the old Latin lacked.

evidence.text: previous to the publication of our recent translation with asterisks and obeli, about seven or eight hundred lines were missing in the Latin,

decisions.reason: Practice taken up: Jerome's own translation carried Origen's critical signs (47020-47022). Wording: the preface is to his newer translation, so the sentence now says the signed version was the earlier one.

decisions.outcome: Narsai founded a new school at Nisibis in Persian lands, and most of the students from the school of Edessa came to him.

evidence.text: il y attira de nombreux frères, de sorte que non seulement les frères persans et syriens venaient à lui, mais encore la plupart des frères qui étaient dans l’école d’Édesse.

decisions.reason: Body formed: Narsai founds the Nisibis school and most of Edessa's students follow (20738-20743). Every fact is in the lines.

decisions.outcome: Calvin made Augustine's teaching on election his own, saying he could set out his whole case in Augustine's words alone.

evidence.text: Were we disposed to frame an entire volume out of Augustine, it were easy to show the reader that I have no occasion to use any other words than his

decisions.reason: Teaching taken up, not just quoted: Calvin says he could build his whole case in Augustine's words (25388-25391), the ruling's own model case.

evidence.text: he excommunicated Sabellius, as not entertaining orthodox opinions.

decisions.reason: One bishop's excommunication (Callistus), reported only by his rival Hippolytus, who says it was done to clear Callistus's name. Not a council, canon, synod or law, and no source shows it held. Rulings: excommunication by one bishop; single hostile witness.

decisions.outcome: Basil defended a disputed form of the doxology as one Gregory the Wonderworker had set, still kept by the church on his authority.

evidence.text: Now one of the institutions of Gregory is the very form of the doxology to which objection is now made, preserved by the Church on the authority of his tradition;

decisions.reason: Practice taken up: the doxology form is Gregory's institution, kept by the church on his authority (14689-14691). The sentence says no more than the lines.

evidence.text: I set to work, as a solace from our troubles, and to relieve the burden of our pilgrimage, to gather into one and arrange all that Origen had written on the book of Numbers,

decisions.reason: One translator's work: Rufinus renders Origen on Numbers 'for the use of our people' (58981-58999). The lines show a text made available, not a church taking it into its Scripture, worship, rule or law. Ruling: translation.

evidence.text: uos certe nobis obicere soletis Cypriani litteras, Cypriani sententiam, Cypriani concilium; cur auctoritatem Cypriani pro uestro schismate adsumitis

decisions.reason: Appeal to an authority: the Donatists cite Cyprian's letters, opinion and council for their schism (10206-10208). The window (to 10150) shows Cyprian's council on rebaptism but not the Donatists adopting that practice. Ruling: appealing to an authority.

decisions.outcome: Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus took their reading of Scripture from Origen's works and turned it against the Arians, Socrates reports.

evidence.text: procured Origen’s works, and drew from them the right interpretation of the sacred Scriptures;

decisions.reason: Teaching taken up: Socrates says they drew their reading of Scripture from Origen's works and used it against the Arians (13913-13922). Attributed to Socrates.

decisions.outcome: The Council in Trullo at Constantinople set its seal on the canons of Gregory the Wonderworker, alongside those of the great councils.

evidence.text: Likewise too the Canons [i.e. the decretal letters] of Dionysius, formerly Archbishop of the great city of Alexandria; and of Peter, Archbishop of Alexandria and Martyr; of Gregory the Wonder-worker, Bishop of Neocæsarea;

decisions.reason: Canon: Trullo canon 2 sets its seal on Gregory's canons as church law (26731-26745).

decisions.outcome: Ephraim set the tunes of Harmonius's songs to orthodox words, and in Theodoret's day those hymns still rang out at the martyrs' festivals.

evidence.text: Ephraim adopted the music of the songs, but set them to piety, and so gave the hearers at once great delight and a healing medicine. These songs are still used to enliven the festivals of our victorious martyrs.

decisions.reason: Practice taken up and lasting: Ephraim set the Bardaisanite tunes to orthodox words and the songs were still sung in Theodoret's day (15063-15066).

decisions.outcome: Meetings of the faithful across Asia judged the New Prophecy heretical, and its followers were expelled from the church and barred from communion.

evidence.text: declared them to be spurious, and rejected them as heretical, they were in consequence of that expelled from the Church and debarred from communion.

decisions.reason: Synods excluding a group: the assemblies of Asia judged the teaching heretical and expelled its followers (11308).

decisions.outcome: Tertullian and his circle broke communion with those he called carnally minded, for their faith in the Paraclete.

evidence.text: We indeed, on our part, subsequently withdrew from the carnally-minded on our acknowledgment and maintenance of the Paraclete.

decisions.reason: Major stands (teaching taken up: Tertullian holds the New Prophecy as the Paraclete's word, 50885-50886, and withdraws over it). But the drafted sentence says he left 'the rest of the church'; the lines say only 'withdrew from the carnally-minded', and the file's own note (51076-51078) says it may mean leaving only the Roman bishop's communion. That fact is not shown.

decisions.outcome: Constantine's law banned Montanist meetings even in private houses and urged them to join the catholic Church instead.

evidence.text: forbid the holding of your superstitious and senseless meetings, not in public merely, but in any private house or place whatsoever. Let those of you, therefore, who are desirous of embracing the true and pure religion, take the far better course of entering the catholic Church,

decisions.reason: Law: Constantine's edict takes their meeting houses and bans their meetings (66124-66130).

decisions.outcome: Justinian ordered the Montanists to give up their faith, Procopius says, and threatened holdouts with losing the right to leave property to their families.

evidence.text: Justinian ordered all these beliefs to be abandoned in favour of the old religion, and threatened the recusants with legal disability to transmit their property to their wives and children by will.

decisions.reason: Law: Justinian's order against the Montanists; Procopius is hostile but the act is public and Novel 45 (59038) names the Montanists too. The sentence names Procopius.

evidence.text: disturbed by the wickedness of an unlawful ordination made in opposition to the Catholic Church, we considered at once that they must be restrained from communion with us;

decisions.reason: Cyprian refusing communion to Novatian's envoys is the quarrel itself. The 'we' who decided is Cyprian's letter; the colleagues in 32599 are waiting for envoys, not shown acting. Ruling: excommunication by one bishop. The lasting result (Nicaea canon 8) is on the imperial-juridical link.

decisions.outcome: The Council of Nicaea let Novatianist clergy keep their rank if they promised in writing to follow the teaching of the Catholic Church.

evidence.text: it is before all things necessary that they should profess in writing that they will observe and follow the dogmas of the Catholic and Apostolic Church;

decisions.reason: Canon: Nicaea canon 8 sets the terms for receiving Novatianist clergy (3769-3775).

decisions.outcome: The church at Rome later threw Marcion out, Tertullian says, and turned away the money he had given it along with him.

evidence.text: he contributed money to the Catholic church, which along with himself was afterwards rejected,

decisions.reason: Exclusion by a church acting as a body: Tertullian says the church rejected Marcion with his gift (29239-29241). Not one bishop alone.

decisions.outcome: The church at Rome expelled Valentinus more than once, Tertullian says, for spreading his ideas among its members.

evidence.text: until on account of their ever restless curiosity, with which they even infected the brethren, they were more than once expelled.

decisions.reason: Exclusion by a church acting as a body: expelled more than once (21338-21339). The dating clash is rightly left out.

decisions.outcome: The meetings at Antioch over Paul of Samosata, which Gregory and Athenodorus joined, ended when a final synod excommunicated him.

evidence.text: Malchion, a Presbyter from the Sophists, was excommunicated.

decisions.reason: Council deposing: the chapter heading (41933-41934) and 'a final synod' (41936) lie within 59 lines of source 1. The drafted sentence implied Gregory sat at the final synod, which the lines do not say; the new wording keeps the two apart. Evidence range widened to include 41936.

decisions.outcome: Eznik and Joseph did the work at Edessa, putting the Scriptures into Armenian from the Syriac and sending the books home.

evidence.text: Ceux-ci se ren- dirent [à Édesse], firent ce qu'on leur avait de- mandé, et, par l'intermédiaire de leurs fidèles compagnons, ils envoyèrent les livres à leurs pères vénérés.

decisions.reason: Translation for the receiving church's common use: Sahak and Mashtots send pupils to Edessa to put the Scriptures into Armenian from the Syriac, and the books are sent home (3839-3845). Ruling: translation.

evidence.text: enjoining on me the task of translating into Latin the ecclesiastical history which was written in the Greek language by that most learned man, Eusebius of Cæsarea. You thought that the mind of those who heard it read to them

decisions.reason: Translation of a history to be read to people in a crisis (58738-58748). Commissioned by a bishop, but for one season's reading, not the church's Scripture, worship, rule or law; no lasting use shown. Ruling: translation.

evidence.text: It is a part of the booty, and in my opinion no small one, which I have carried off from the libraries of the Greeks, and which I am collecting for the use and advantage of our countrymen.

decisions.reason: One translator's work for 'our countrymen' (58596-58601), addressed to Gaudentius; no church shown taking it up. Ruling: translation.

decisions.outcome: Augustine set out Tyconius's seven rules in his own handbook and urged students to read the book, though with care over its Donatist errors.

evidence.text: in order both that the book may be read by the studious (for it is of very great assistance in understanding Scripture), and that no more may be expected from it than it really contains.

decisions.reason: Rule taken up: Augustine sets out Tyconius's seven rules in his own handbook (53080) and tells students to read the book (53074-53077), within 42 lines of source 1. More than praise.

decisions.outcome: Benedict's Rule named the Lives of the Fathers among the books one monk read aloud to the whole community after supper.

evidence.text: sedeant omnes in unum, et legat unus Collationes, vel Vitas Patrum

decisions.reason: Set reading in a rule (6836-6841). The drafted sentence put the Conferences on this link too; they belong to the Cassian link. Each link now carries only its own text.

decisions.outcome: Cassian set down Egypt's monastic customs so a bishop in Gaul could establish them in his new monastery, in a province then without monasteries.

evidence.text: you are anxious that the institutions of the East and especially of Egypt should be established in your province, which is at present without monasteries,

decisions.reason: Practice taken up for a new Gallic house (16433-16448), and Gennadius has Cassian founding two monasteries at Marseilles (43243-43246). Castor's name comes only from the editor's endnote (16435-16437), so it is dropped; 'Gaul' is in the reviewed note.

decisions.outcome: Benedict's Rule had one monk read the Conferences aloud to the whole community each evening, and again before Compline on fast days.

evidence.text: mox accedant ad lectionem Collationum, ut diximus

decisions.reason: Set reading in a rule: the Conferences after supper and on fast days after Vespers (6839-6846); Compline follows at 6851-6852, inside the window. Not a duplicate of the desert link: the Rule names a different text.

decisions.outcome: An imperial law of July 381 forbade Eunomians to build churches in town or country and seized any land where they did.

evidence.text: nullum eunomianorum atque arrianorum vel ex dogmate aeti in civitate vel agris fabricandarum ecclesiarum copiam habere praecipimus.

decisions.reason: Law excluding the group, with land seized (7064).

decisions.outcome: The bishops whom Theodosius gathered at Constantinople anathematized the Semi-Arians, also called Pneumatomachi, in their first canon.

evidence.text: and that of the Semi-Arians or Pneumatomachi

decisions.reason: Council canon condemning the group by name (13965-13976).

decisions.outcome: A law of March 388 drove the Apollinarians from the cities and stripped their bishops of the title of bishop.

evidence.text: nulla his episcoporum faciendorum praebeatur auctoritas; ipsi quoque episcopi nomine destituti appellationem dignitatis huius amittant.

decisions.reason: Law excluding the group and stripping its bishops' title (7080).

decisions.outcome: Hilarion brought the monk's way of life to Palestine, where no monasteries had stood, and was the first to train men in it there.

evidence.text: For as yet there were no monasteries in Palestine, nor had anyone known a monk in Syria before the saintly Hilarion. It was he who originated this mode of life and devotion, and who first trained men to it in that province.

decisions.reason: Practice taken up and a new body: Hilarion, Antony's visitor (30141-30143), first trained men in the monk's life in Palestine (30347-30350).

decisions.outcome: The bishops of Gaul refused communion to Saturninus and condemned the creed sent to them from Sirmium as soon as it arrived.

evidence.text: you had denied him communion for the whole three years ago until now. I equally rejoiced that the impious and infidel creed which was sent straightway to you from Sirmium was not only not accepted by you, but condemned

decisions.reason: A body of bishops condemning a creed: Hilary credits the bishops of Gaul, together, with condemning the Sirmium creed (7776-7779). Unlike Cyprian's case, the act is the bishops' as a body and it condemns a teaching.

evidence.text: imposed a form of faith upon the churches. Opposing bishops they drove into exile.

decisions.reason: Exile of opposing bishops, Hilary among them (9519-9523). The same passage says the emperor later admitted his error, and Hilary returned; no lasting result shown. Ruling: exile soon reversed.

decisions.outcome: An imperial law of July 383 banned Arians, along with Eunomians and other groups, from meeting or gathering any crowd.

evidence.text: eunomiani, arriani, macedoniani, pneumatomachi manichaei, encratitae, apotactitae, saccofori, hydroparastatae nullis circulis coeant

decisions.reason: Law excluding the group (7074). A different law from the Eunomian link's, so not a duplicate.

decisions.outcome: A council of nineteen bishops at Rome, granted by Constantine, condemned Donatus and cleared his rival Caecilian.

evidence.text: It is, therefore, sufficient, that Donatus was condemned by the verdict of so many Bishops, and that Caecilian was cleared by the judgement of so great an authority.

decisions.reason: Council deposing: the nineteen bishops at Rome condemn Donatus and clear Caecilian (273-285). Optatus is hostile, but he quotes the council's own verdict, a public act.

decisions.outcome: The Persian bishops agreed to serve the liturgy by the western order that Bishops Isaac and Marutha had taught them at Seleucia.

evidence.text: nous exercerons tous uniformément le ministère selon le ministère occidental que les évèques Isaac et Marouta nous ont enseigné

decisions.reason: Practice taken up by synod: the Persian bishops adopt the western order of worship (17202-17204).

decisions.outcome: A law of July 381 ordered every church handed to bishops in communion with Helladius of Caesarea and Gregory of Nyssa, among others.

evidence.text: in pontica dioecesi helladio episcopo caesariensi et otreio meliteno et gregorio episcopo nysseno

decisions.reason: Law: communion with named Cappadocian bishops becomes the legal test for holding churches (6887). The same law also names Diodore; it names both parties in its own words, so both links keep it. Ruling: duplicates.

evidence.text: They have expelled my brother from Nyssa, and into his place have introduced hardly a man

decisions.reason: Gregory's expulsion from Nyssa (40975-40976): Basil names no agent and no synod, the Homoian identity rests on editors' headnotes, and the expulsion was later undone. Ruling: exile soon reversed.

decisions.outcome: Ambrose won a promise from Theodosius to amend his edict on the burned synagogue and to end the whole investigation.

evidence.text: he said that he would amend the edict. I went on at once to say that he must end the whole investigation,

decisions.reason: Rule changed: Theodosius promises to amend the edict and end the inquiry (43980-43990), and says the order 'has been rectified' (43971-43973). Ambrose's own account, of a public act.

decisions.outcome: A law of July 381 ordered every church handed to bishops in communion with Diodore of Tarsus and others it named.

evidence.text: in orientis partibus pelagio episcopo laodicensi et diodoro episcopo tarsensi

decisions.reason: Law: communion with Diodore of Tarsus named as a legal test (6887). Same law as the Cappadocian link; it names both parties. Ruling: duplicates.

decisions.outcome: After synods condemned John Chrysostom, his followers, called Johannites, left the church and held their own assemblies apart.

evidence.text: from that time held their assemblies apart in various places, and were from him denominated ‘Johannites.’

decisions.reason: Separate body formed: the Johannites hold their own assemblies (18487-18495).

decisions.outcome: The Second Council of Constantinople cursed Theodore of Mopsuestia and all who defended him or called his reading of Scripture orthodox.

evidence.text: if anyone does not anathematize him or his impious writings, as well as all those who protect or defend him, or who assert that his exegesis is orthodox,

decisions.reason: Council condemning a teacher and his writings (23937-23939).

decisions.outcome: A synod of the Church of the East defended the books and teaching of Theodore and refuted those who spread lies about him.

evidence.text: Apologie pour les livres et la doctrine de saint Théodore, et réfatation des hérétiques qui lui firent une réputation mensongère.

decisions.reason: Teaching taken up by synod: the 585 canon is an apology for Theodore's books and teaching (26570-26571).

decisions.outcome: At Aquileia the bishops condemned Palladius, judged him unworthy of the priesthood and ordered a Catholic bishop ordained in his place.

evidence.text: pronuncio illum facerdo- tio indignum & * carendum; & in loco ejus catholicus ordinetur, Omnes epifcop! dixerunr: Anathema Palladio .

decisions.reason: Council deposing: Palladius judged unworthy, a Catholic to be ordained in his place, all the bishops assenting (60888-60911).

decisions.outcome: The Council of Trent declared the old Latin Vulgate the authentic text for public lectures, debates, sermons and expositions, and let no one reject it.

evidence.text: the  said  old  and  Vulgate  edition,  which,  by the  lengthened  usage  of  so  many  ages,  has  been  approved  of  in the  Church,  be,  in  public  lectures,  disputations,  sermons,  and expositions,  held  as  authentic

decisions.reason: Text taken up by a council: Trent declares the old Vulgate authentic (12477-12482). The tie to Jerome rests on listed sources 1 and 2.

decisions.outcome: Justinian forbade Donatists, Arians, Jews and pagans to keep meeting places or hold rites in the manner of the church.

evidence.text: Neque enim Iudaeos neque paganos neque Donatistas neque Árianos neque alios quoscumque haereticos vel speluncas habere vel quaedam quasi ritu ecclesiastico facere patimur,

decisions.reason: Law excluding the group (52635-52637).

decisions.outcome: Once the case was reported to the palace, the emperor decreed that Priscillian and his friends be put to death.

evidence.text: the emperor decreed that Priscillian and his friends should be put to death.

decisions.reason: Imperial sentence on the group's leaders (11673-11674), after Gratian's rescript drove them out (11529-11531). A public act.

decisions.outcome: Ulfila, bishop of the Goths, gave his assent to the creed of Constantinople, though he had once held to the creed of Nicaea.

evidence.text: To this creed Ulfilas bishop of the Goths gave his assent, although he had previously adhered to that of Nicæa;

decisions.reason: Teaching taken up: Ulfila of the Goths assents to the creed of Constantinople (9608-9610); Maximinus still holds the Ariminum creed in 427 or 428 (source 3). Not the same event as the 383 law on the other link of this pair.

evidence.text: They further threatened that they would withdraw from his communion, travel to the western empire, and publish his plots to the world. Leontius was now alarmed, and suspended Aetius from his sacred office,

decisions.reason: Aetius's suspension, but the same lines say Leontius 'continued to show him marked favour' (10455-10456). Ruling: exile or suspension soon reversed.

decisions.outcome: Counsels credited to Antony the Great stand first, after the preface, in the Philokalia, the Greek collection of writings on prayer.

evidence.text: Τοῦ ἐν ᾿Αγίοις Πατρὸς ἡμῶν ᾿Αν- τωνίου τοῦ Μεγάλου, παραινέσεις

decisions.reason: Compilation: the Philokalia that Nikodemos and Macarius issued (source 1, 147-153) opens, after its preface, with Antony's counsels (58621-58628). Ruling: compilation.

decisions.outcome: On Severus's advice, Dioscorus of Alexandria won back men who had long refused communion, and they joined the Egyptian church.

evidence.text: as far as was possible he complied with my advice and satisfied those who were separated

decisions.reason: Settlement changed: a long-separated party rejoins the Egyptian church when Dioscorus follows Severus's advice (5202-5214). Severus is the only witness, but the reunion is a public act.

decisions.outcome: Reparatus of Carthage lost his office and was sent into exile for refusing to condemn the Three Chapters, and his own envoy was made bishop in his place.

evidence.text: Reparatus archiepiscopus plurimis calumniis inipetitus pro eo, quod damnationi trium memoratorum capitulorum assensimi non praebuit, officio sumptibusque privatus Euchaida exilio relegatur, ct Primosus diaconus apocrisarius eius

decisions.reason: Deposition with a successor installed (19068-19072). The year 552 is the drafters' own count from Victor's regnal heading, not a date the text gives, so it is dropped.

decisions.outcome: Justinian's law ordered every copy of Severus's writings burned and barred him from the capital and its district.

evidence.text: sed sint profana et aliena ab ecclesia catholica igneque comburantur a possidentibus

decisions.reason: Law: Severus's books to be burned, Severus barred from the capital (56691-56695). The pair also has a 'broke with' link, but that carries Severus's flight in 518, a different event.

decisions.outcome: A synod at Dvin in 554, under Catholicos Nerses II, confirmed the Armenian church's refusal of Chalcedon and proclaimed the faith of Ephesus against it.

evidence.text: at the synod of Douine (554), at which the faith, as decreed at Ephesus, was emphatically proclaimed in opposition to Nestorian errors and Chalcedonian claims.

decisions.reason: Synod rejecting the other side's council. Secondary only, but the reviewed note states it and the vendored Ormanian lines (2550-2556) show it. Ruling: secondary evidence.

decisions.outcome: Nerses Bakur, head of the Albanian church, was removed for leaning toward communion with the Greek church, and Simeon took his place.

evidence.text: Their patriarch, Nerses Bakour, tempted by the example of Kurion, inclined to the side of communion with the Greek Church. He was immediately removed and replaced by Simeon.

decisions.reason: Deposition and replacement of Albania's head. Secondary only; note states it and vendored Ormanian (2902-2907) shows it. No agent is named, and the sentence names none.

decisions.outcome: The Georgian church accepted the Council of Chalcedon, and its head later stood on that council's side with bishops from the Greek lands.

evidence.text: Tenaient le parti de Chalcldoine le catholicos de G^orgie et d'Albanie avec beaucoup d'6v6ques de la region grecque

decisions.reason: Teaching taken up: Georgia's head on Chalcedon's side (Sebeos, 7441-7443); the acceptance itself is stated in the note and in vendored Ormanian (2716-2724).

decisions.outcome: In 802 Charlemagne ordered that whatever monasteries did against the Rule of Saint Benedict be put right by that rule.

evidence.text: quicquid in monasteriis seu in 15 monachis contra regula sancti Benedicti factum fuisset, hoc ipsud iuxta ipsam regulam sancti Benedicti emendare fecissent.

decisions.reason: Rule imposed by imperial order (7794-7805); Carloman's 742 canon (2324-2325) also.

evidence.text: disproving that same book which he had written concerning the resurrection, determined that it ought to be consumed in the flames.

decisions.reason: The emperor's judgment came in a private audience, reported only by Gregory, a party to the dispute; Eutychius's recantation is hearsay ('as I learnt from their relation', 8501-8503). No council or law, and no lasting result in either church. Ruling: single hostile witness.

evidence.text: save that with respect to those who attain to the episcopate from among the Donatists, we by all means forbid them to be advanced to the dignity of primacy,

decisions.reason: A ruling in a letter (33811-33819) with no sign it was carried out; the letter mostly leaves the Numidian custom as it was. Ruling: ruling in a letter.

decisions.outcome: A Carolingian list of what clergy must learn named Gregory's pastoral book among the texts every canon had to know.

evidence.text: 13. Librum pastoralem* canonici atque librum officiorum;

decisions.reason: Set reading in a rule: canons must know the pastoral book (16128). The identification as Gregory's is the edition's footnote (16138) and the reviewed note.

decisions.outcome: King Alfred had Gregory's Pastoral Rule rendered into West Saxon English, meaning to send a copy to every bishop in his kingdom.

evidence.text: made a translation, or rather paraphrase, of it in the West Saxon tongue, intending, as he says, to send a copy to every bishop in his Kingdom

decisions.reason: Translation for the receiving church's common use: made by the king with his divines, meant for every bishop. Secondary, but the note states it and vendored Barmby (24031-24035) shows it; the sentence keeps 'meaning to'.

decisions.outcome: Justinian barred every Christian outside the orthodox faith from baptism and the other sacraments, and Arian soldiers in the Roman army joined a mutiny over it.
